title: NoBrainerWagers Review 2026: Pricing, Record, Worth It?
description: NoBrainerWagers review, checked 7 Nov 2026: prices from $299 a week to $9,999 lifetime, what its 2026 pick log shows, a closed lawsuit and buyer reports.
dek: NoBrainerWagers sells picks from $299 a week to $9,999 for life, delivered through private Telegram channels. It publishes a 2026 pick log that matches its headline record, but the log has no time stamps and nothing before 2026. Buyer reviews are mostly glowing, with clustered posting dates and repeated refund complaints.

status.label: Not verified
status.note: Watchdog has not graded a full, time stamped record for NoBrainerWagers. This page reports what we could check and labels everything else.

short_answer: NoBrainerWagers is a real, active business. It names an LLC, publishes its prices, sells through its own site and through Whop, and sends picks in private Telegram channels. It also publishes a log of every 2026 pick with wins, losses and pushes, which is more than many social media sellers show.

Whether it makes money for buyers is less clear. The 2026 log adds up to the record on the homepage, 434-307-22 and +169.8 units, but it has no time each pick was sent, about 38% of entries have no odds, and nothing before 2026 is posted. The ten year win rate and the 892% average annual return in its Whop FAQ are seller claims with no log behind them that we could open.

Buyer reviews split sharply. Most are five stars, but many arrived in bursts on single days, and the negative ones repeat the same complaints: promised refunds on guaranteed picks that never came, unwanted renewals and constant upsells. A customer's 2025 federal lawsuit against the company was voluntarily dismissed in December 2025 with no ruling. If you buy, buy short and record every pick with the line you actually got.
pricing_intro: Prices below were shown on nobrainerwagers.com and on the NoBrainerWagers Whop store on 7 Nov 2026. The two price lists differ slightly. After payment, Whop says buyers are added to private Telegram channels where the picks are released.
pricing: $299 a week (site and Whop), 2 to 7 bets daily
Auto renews until cancelled. Charges already made are non refundable except as required by law or under the posted Refund Policy
$2,750 a year on the site. $2,749 a year on Whop, shown as 20% off $3,436.25
Same as above. Excludes VIP, Locks of the Year and Locks of the Month
$3,500 a year on the site, one MAX bet a day of 6% to 12% of bankroll, includes standard packages. Whop lists a VIP Pick of the Day at $3,499 a year and a Mortal Lock Package at $3,500 a year
$9,999 one time, all sports and packages "for the tenure of business operations"
Sold as a one time purchase. Whop FAQ: all purchases final
guarantee: We found no performance guarantee and no refund policy page. The site's renewal terms say memberships renew automatically, that you cancel by emailing support, and that amounts already charged are non refundable "except as required by law or under the posted Refund Policy," but the refund policy address we tried returned a not found page. The Whop FAQ is blunter: "all purchases are final."

Several buyers describe one off "guaranteed" picks or packages that promised money back or a free package if the pick lost, and say the refund never came. Those are customer reports, listed below. We did not see the terms of those offers ourselves.

claims.claim: Plays sent only when the algorithm finds "a 70% or higher projected edge"

claims_note: A 70% "projected edge" is not a standard betting term, and the log does not show anything close to a 70% hit rate. The posted 2026 record wins 58.6% of decided picks, at mostly short favorite prices.
The account growth number is the unit total times 3. It assumes every unit is 3% of a fixed starting bank and ignores the price of the membership.

The VIP play is described as 6% to 12% of a bettor's total bankroll on one game. Most bankroll guides treat that as very aggressive sizing, since a short losing run can take a large share of the bank.
The scrolling ticker at the top of the homepage shows wins and losses with no dates, so it cannot be checked against anything.
record: What a buyer can check outside the seller: nothing independent. We found no third party monitor, contest result or regulator record of NoBrainerWagers picks.

What is the seller's own record: the site's bet history page loads a data feed of every 2026 pick. On 7 Nov 2026 it held 763 entries from 1 Jan to 4 Nov 2026, totaling 434 wins, 307 losses and 22 pushes for +169.75 units, which matches the homepage. 290 entries had no odds and 306 had no game start time, and no entry showed when the pick was sent, so the feed cannot prove a pick went out before the game. Of the 472 entries with odds, about 96% were favorites, with a median price of -120. By month the log was positive from January through September and negative in October (about -7.2 units) and early November (about -6.7 units). The homepage showed 40.0% over the last 10 graded picks. No picks from before 2026 are posted, despite the claim of operating since 2017.

Court record: federal court records list Sheeler v. Nobrainerwagers, LLC, case 9:25-cv-80739 in the Southern District of Florida, filed 12 Jun 2025 by a self represented plaintiff against the company and one individual, with the nature of suit listed as "Other Fraud." The defendants moved to dismiss. The plaintiff filed a notice of voluntary dismissal on 30 Dec 2025 and the court closed the case on 31 Dec 2025. No court ruled on the claims, and we did not read the complaint.

our_data.text: Watchdog grades picks captured from public posts before the game starts. In this edition NoBrainerWagers is not matched to a Watchdog graded record, so we make no claim about how its picks perform.
our_data.context: For scale: NoBrainerWagers advertises a ten year win rate of 63.9%. On the Watchdog board on 7 Nov 2026, {{over60}} of {{established}} established accounts (100 or more graded picks) were at 60% or better, and the median established account won {{median_win}}% of its picks. At standard -110 odds a bettor needs about 52.4% to break even.

customers_intro: NoBrainerWagers has a large review file, and most of it is five stars. The file also shows reviews arriving in bursts on single days, five star Whop reviews written minutes after purchase, and a steady line of complaints about refunds and upsells. Below is what we read and how much weight it can carry.

customers.text: Trustpilot showed 88 reviews and a 4.0 score, with 85% five star and 14% one star. On the first page of 20, about a dozen reviews were posted on 26 Mar 2026, and the company replied to each of them that same day. Trustpilot noted the company had not replied to negative reviews.

A one star Trustpilot reviewer said his card was charged for two more months of a subscription he did not want, that he was told the money was sent back but never received it, and that the support email did not work.

A Trustpilot reviewer said he paid $500 for a guaranteed set of picks that lost, and that NoBrainerWagers ignored him on Telegram and Instagram for four days instead of refunding as promised. He said he had spent about $5,000 with the service in total.
A Trustpilot reviewer on the VIP and base packages said he was up overall, had losing days, and that it is not a get rich quick product.
An anonymized one star Trustpilot reviewer called the service a scam, claimed it falsifies its record, and said it tries to upsell buyers almost daily. These are the reviewer's claims, not findings.

A CapperTek reviewer claimed the service offers a free "500 dollar" pick for good reviews and cut off his membership after he complained. He said he spent around $20,000 or more on a lifetime plan plus separate sport packages, that a paid Telegram group was deleted, and that a promised free Super Bowl package was not delivered. He also said the picks lay an average of about -150.

A CapperTek reviewer called the picks decent but said the reporting was only about 90% accurate, claiming some losses were counted as pushes and a losing Wimbledon package was left off the record. He described 6 or 7 Telegram channels with around 30 alerts a day, an "all inclusive" lifetime plan followed by extra paid packages, and an unpaid refund on a money back offer.

A CapperTek reviewer who bought the monthly pick of the day, props and parlay packages said the pick of the day hit about 60%, the parlay package posted only 21 parlays in about ten weeks, and support stopped answering once he raised concerns.

Most of the 43 CapperTek reviews are positive. Long time members praise quick replies, the bankroll system, and results posted win or lose, and several say the high price scared them before it paid off. Thirteen of the 43 are dated 30 Sep 2024 and six more 15 Dec 2022, and one 30 Sep 2024 review opens with the same words as a Trustpilot review from that date.
The Whop store showed 11 ratings, all five stars. The four reviews on display were each marked as written between 2 and 34 minutes after purchase, one claiming a steady 60% to 65% win rate.

SmartCustomer (formerly SiteJabber) showed no reviews, the Better Business Bureau search returned no results for No Brainer Wagers, and we found no Reddit, TheRX, SBR or Covers forum thread about the service.

conflicts: The homepage promotes Novig as "the book we bet through" with the promo code NBW and a $50 bonus, and says NoBrainerWagers "may receive a referral benefit." A seller paid when readers sign up has a reason to send them to that book.
The site sells the picks and also publishes the only record of how they did. No outside party grades the log.
One customer review claims free picks were offered in exchange for good reviews. We could not confirm that, but it is a reason to weigh the review file carefully.
strengths: A public log of every 2026 pick, losses and pushes included, that adds up to the advertised record.
Published prices, a free daily play, and auto renewal terms written on the site.
Many long time buyers praise fast replies and clear bankroll rules.
concerns: The log has no time each pick was sent, many entries lack odds, and nothing before 2026 is posted. The ten year and 892% claims are unsupported.
All purchases are final, and buyers repeatedly report guaranteed picks whose promised refunds never came.
Recurring complaints about upsells, separate packages on top of "all inclusive" plans, and unwanted renewals.
VIP plays sized at 6% to 12% of a bankroll are very aggressive.
A sportsbook referral deal on the homepage, and review bursts on single days on CapperTek and Trustpilot.
checklist: Ask for every pick from the last 12 months with the line, the odds and the time it was sent. A list of hot runs is not a record.
Count units, not wins. A 60% record at heavy favorites can still lose money.
Read the guarantee for the words refund, credit and extension. Most "guarantees" in this business are credits.
Write down each pick yourself the moment you receive it, with the line you can actually get.
Give any handicapper a few hundred picks before you call them a winner. Short runs swing hard both ways.
faq: It is a real business with a named LLC, published prices and a public 2026 pick log, and many buyers say they received what they paid for. It also has repeated refund complaints and a 2025 fraud lawsuit by a customer that was voluntarily dismissed in December 2025 without any ruling.

On 7 Nov 2026 standard memberships were $299 a week, $699 a month, $1,499 for six months and $2,750 a year on its site, with VIP at $3,500 a year and lifetime at $9,999. Memberships auto renew, and Whop says all purchases are final.
Does NoBrainerWagers have a verified record?

No. It publishes its own 2026 log of 763 picks at 434-307-22 and +169.75 units, but the log has no posting times and nothing before 2026, no outside party grades it, and Watchdog has no graded record for it.

For the money you get 2 to 7 picks a day, mostly favorites, through Telegram, plus bankroll guidance. What is unproven is whether a buyer, getting the line available at release, beats the roughly 52.4% needed at -110 over time after paying $299 a week or more, and there is no refund if the picks lose.
